newsitem.title: USA: U.S. voters find presidential debate disappointing.
newsitem.headline: U.S. voters find presidential debate disappointing.

text.p: Sunday's presidential debate did little to shed light on the important issues facing the United States less than one month before the election, a politically mixed group of voters concluded.

All but two of the 15 voters assembled to watch and discuss the 90-minute debate ranked the clash between Democratic President Bill Clinton and Republican challenger Bob Dole at one on a scale of 1-10.
Reflecting a dissatisfied U.S. electorate, the voters said they were frustrated by the lack of new issues and a suspicion that neither candidate was telling the full truth.

"What I found in the debate was the candidates seemed to be speaking what we already knew about almost every issue," said Debby Yager, 47, an unemployed Philadelphia resident who described herself as a Clinton supporter.
"There was almost nothing new in the debate. There was the party line, or the Bill Clinton line, or the Bob Dole line."
Alcide Gaboriault, 66, a retired Unisys employee and undecided Republican, said: "Everytime somebody said something, (the opponent) would say the opposite. So who was lying?"

"They say they've got a tax plan; tell me how they're going to do it," said Judy Rice, 62, a retired schoolteacher and Clinton supporter. "They say they've put 100,000 police on the streets; show me where they are."

The session was organised at Villanova University in suburban Philadelphia by communications professor David LeVasseur, under the auspices of DebateWatch '96, a national group sponsored by the Commission on Presidential Debates.
Results were gathered from dozens of debate meetings across the country on Sunday with the aim of improving future presidential campaign debates.
Participants said education and the issue of school choice was the debate topic that stood out most and pointed to the broader issue of the role of government in the United States.

"School is just one aspect of personal choice...I don't want the federal government telling me what I should do," said Robert Montgomery, 45, a Dole supporter who described himself as a child of the 1960s and eager for a debate with "passion."

Clinton and Dole's differing positions on taxes also drew strong interest, with several participants remarking on Dole's assertion that Americans were working harder and paying a greater share of their income in taxes than ever before.
Participants said the presidential candidates avoided the issue of women's rights, and failed to address the question of corporate takeovers and buyouts.

The voters, aged 19 to 79, said more specific questioning of the candidates was needed, either by partisan questioners or persons able to challenge claims made by the candidates with statistics and research.
Clinton was praised for being more specific than Dole in his answers, while Dole came across better than expected.
Both candidates won points for their civil conduct during the debate in which they made few personal attacks.
A questionnaire filled out by the participants revealed that the debate did not change the way they will vote, but did serve to reinforce attitudes about the candidates.
